description: We're students from UW participating in this hackathon!
summary:
Space games for kids feel like homework. Games are either too hard or too easy, and most importantly they don't give kids a reason to come back.
Our solution? Look to the games they already play for inspiration. Kids already balance complex decision-making in the games they play on popular game sites like Roblox. 
Moon Base Trainer takes the aspects kids love and turns it educational. Progress is saved and rewarded through level progression, so kids have a reason to keep playing and exploring. In addition, students still practice critical thinking when they make decisions and consider trade-offs. Lastly, our game is grounded in real data and research, so that teachers know that their students get information they rely on.
We hope you enjoy Moon Base Trainer, and game on!
details:
Moon Base Trainer is a free browser game for kids 7 to 12, where you run a small base at Connecting Ridge near the Moon’s south pole. Students use the habitat's many stations to keep three meters balanced: power, life support and radiation, as well as completing objectives. Every helpful action has a cost, so each choice matters. Clearing a mission earns stars and research points that unlock new missions.

We designed Moon Base Trainer with modern game-development in mind: we want kids to have a reason to come back and learn more, which we don't see much in current games. The core of the game is a level-based design and research tree, where progress is saved and rewarded. The main gameplay loop is a 3D simulator game where students consider trade-offs, make decisions, and finally return with progression - something to show for their efforts.

An educational game shouldn't feel like homework: learning should be exciting and fresh, and the game shouldn't hold your hand for too long or be too punishing. What's more, parents and teachers should know that the game has information they can trust. That's why our game incorporates all these aspects through the real NASA research and data we present to the students. Levels are separated in 3 difficulties for different ages, and information is presented in a way anyone can understand. Our Scrapbook glossary contains two levels of reading so that students feel engaged while they learn, and our futuristic design aims to keep science fresh and exciting.

We prioritized accessibility, which is why our game is built in-browser on a fast-loading engine. We used JavaScript, Vite, and three.js to build our browser game, as well as Rapier for physics. Python helped us process NASA data, including the maps, solar information, and astronaut health data. We also used NASA models for reference, and simplified them in Blender to match our aesthetic. We used Claude to assist with code development, game balancing, Blender, fact checks, text, and the music. The team made the research, design choices, and tested the game.

Real NASA data and research drives the game while the format is something that kids are already familiar with. This gives our project the benefit of education and engagement. Our team considered age fit, making sure that concepts are understandable and difficulty is adjusted. We also considered access, settling on a web game since platforms like Roblox require accounts and screening, as well as accessibility, with contrasting text and two reading levels. Lastly, our priority was scientific accuracy, which was double-checked between NASA sources when being implemented.
